name: Olga Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the small business team at Meridian, out at the business park past the ring road. We insure cafés, hair salons, little workshops, that kind of thing. My part is the paperwork: renewals, changes to cover when someone buys a new oven or moves premises, and sending the policy documents out to the brokers, who sell the policies to the businesses. It's fiddly but I like that each file is a real little business with a story.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The endorsements, which are the small changes added to a policy, like covering a new van. I miss details, and Callum, who trained me, sends files back with yellow sticky notes. I use the AI assistant now and then to double-check wording, once I saw Callum do it. Home is a flat with my partner Dario, who's a chef, and my sister Nadia and I own a second little flat that we rent out, so money's okay even though Dario's restaurant hours go up and down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but not useless, which is what I'd say about most things. At work I'd probably say thank goodness, now can we fix the printer. Online I wouldn't say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's fine in that world, I think. What I'd still worry about is Dario. The restaurant my partner works at cut his shifts twice this year, and that's got nothing to do with AI. With prices where they are, people eat out less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Meridian and try to get off Callum's sticky-note list, maybe by doing the commercial insurance certificate next year. I'd keep saving, and Nadia and I would keep the rented flat. If Dario's hours dropped again, my wage would carry us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with a background hum of worry about Dario's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dario say if his shifts dropped again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he'll find another kitchen, and he would, because good chefs always do. But he'd be grumpy for a month and we'd stop going out. That's the pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the bit of automation touch your desk at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. Sending out the documents and chasing brokers for missing details, a program could do some of that. I'd probably end up with more of the tricky changes, which is where I make mistakes, so I'd need to get better at those.

say: I'd say AI was **overhyped but not useless**.
At work I'd joke that now we can finally **fix the printer**.
think: My job is **fine** in that world, I think.
My real worry is Dario, whose **restaurant shifts** were cut twice this year.
do: Take the **commercial insurance certificate** next year.
Keep the **rented flat** with Nadia and keep saving.
Cover household costs with her wage if Dario's **hours drop**.
feel: **Mostly steady**, with a **background hum** of worry about Dario's job.
S0.quote: The restaurant my partner works at cut his shifts twice this year, and that's got nothing to do with AI.
fieldNote: Olga's unease in this world comes from **hospitality**, not technology.
She sees that small automation would leave her the **tricky changes**, her weakest area.
Her **half-share** of a **rented flat** gives the household a real cushion.

steps.text: Keep processing small business renewals at Meridian
Take the commercial insurance certificate next year
Keep saving and keep the rented flat with Nadia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's be sensible about it. Firms should bring tools in with training, and people should give them a fair go. I wouldn't be on either side shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my desk is right in the path. Renewals, documents, chasing brokers: that's checking and writing and answering customers. They won't need ten of us on the small business team; maybe four, and the four will be the ones who are good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch which colleagues get on well with the new system, then ask them to show me, and take the firm's training as soon as there's proof it's working. I'd ask Callum about moving up to underwriting assistant, where you help decide whether to insure a business at all. And I'd put a bit more aside every month in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I've got the rented flat and savings, so losing my job would be a slope, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does an underwriting assistant do differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They look at a bakery and decide what could go wrong and how much to charge, instead of just typing up the result. It needs judgement, and I'd hope that's the part they keep people for longer. I don't know for sure, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe four of ten. Who'd you bet on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum, obviously, and Priyanka, who already uses every tool going. Then two out of the rest of us. Honestly, on my current form, I wouldn't bet on me keeping my job on the small business team, which is why I'd move.

say: I'd say it's happening, so let's be **sensible** about it.
Firms should **train people**, and people should give the tools a fair go.
think: My desk is **right in the path**: renewals, documents and chasing brokers.
The team may shrink from **ten to four**, keeping only the good ones.
do: Take the firm's **AI training** once colleagues show it works.
Ask Callum about moving up to **underwriting assistant**.
Put a bit **more aside** every month.
feel: **Anxious but not frozen**, since savings make this a slope, not a cliff.
S1.quote: I've got the rented flat and savings, so losing my job would be a slope, not a cliff.
fieldNote: Olga's centre outlook shows in **no blame**: she wants firms and staff both to be sensible.
She **wouldn't bet on herself** keeping her seat, and plans to move up instead.
Her **steady habit** is clear: learn from colleagues first, then adopt.

steps.text: Take Meridian's AI training once colleagues show it works
Apply to move up to underwriting assistant
Put a bit more of each wage into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments to buy people time, maybe by making firms phase it in, and some kind of income for people in between. I'd say it calmly, at work and to friends. I wouldn't be at protests, but I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's gone within two years, and so is underwriting, probably. If AI can do any thinking job, insurance is finished as a place for people like me. The odd thing is Dario's job might be the safer one for once, because robots for kitchens come about three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Dario and seriously look at opening a small catering business together, him cooking and me doing the books, bookings and licences until AI does those too. We'd use my savings and maybe sell my half of the rented flat to Nadia for the start-up money. I'd stay at Meridian until they let me go and keep the redundancy money for a year of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years is too fast to do anything well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling your half of the flat to your sister. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia would say yes, but she'd make me promise it's not a mad idea. And I couldn't promise that, not in two years. I'd tell her my partner and I are betting on people still wanting a real cook at their wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come for kitchen work around 2031. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're three years in and either we've built something people want from a person, or we haven't. A wedding caterer who knows the family might last longer than a factory kitchen. But I'm guessing, really.

say: I'd say governments must **buy people time** by making firms phase it in.
I'd call for an **income in between** jobs, and vote on it.
think: My job is **gone within two years**, along with underwriting.
Dario's **kitchen job** may be safer, since robots come about three years later.
do: Plan a **catering business** with Dario, him cooking, her doing the books.
Sell her **half of the flat** to Nadia for start-up money.
Stay until laid off and keep the **redundancy money** for rent.
feel: **Scared**, because two years is **too fast** to do anything well.
S2.quote: My partner and I are betting on people still wanting a real cook at their wedding.
fieldNote: Fast AGI flips the household: Dario's **hands-on job** becomes the safer one.
Olga is willing to **cash in property** to build something with her partner.
She is honest that the catering plan is **a guess**, not a sure thing.

steps.text: Start a small wedding catering business with Dario
Put savings and flat money into catering equipment
Ask her sister Nadia to buy out her half of the flat
Keep the redundancy money aside for a year of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, if people are honest with each other. I'd want firms to give clear dates and help people move. I'd say that at work, nicely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job goes around 2030, I'd guess. That gives me time to try the catering idea on weekends before betting the flat on it. And Dario's kitchen work lasts until about 2034, so the hands-on side buys us a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Meridian and save, and from next spring we'd do private dinners and small parties at weekends to test the catering idea. If it worked by 2029, I'd go part-time and do a short business and food-safety course. We'd only sell the flat share if the weekends were clearly paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the useful kind. Testing first suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a first weekend job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a fortieth birthday for one of Dario's old regulars, thirty people, lamb and a big salad. I'd do the quote, the shopping list, the timings. If I hated it, I'd know early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back from, even with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Children, probably. My partner and I talked about starting a family around 2029, and I'd want to see what our income looks like first. That's the thing I'd actually put off.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to plan if people are honest.
Firms should give **clear dates** and help people move.
think: My job goes around **2030**, leaving time to test catering first.
Dario's kitchen work lasts until about **2034**, which buys us years.
do: Cater **weekend dinners and parties** from next spring as a test.
Go **part-time** and take a business and **food-safety course** by 2029 if it works.
Sell the **flat share** only if the weekends clearly pay.
feel: **Anxious** in a **useful** way, because testing first suits her.
S3.quote: My partner and I talked about starting a family around 2029, and I'd want to see what our income looks like first.
fieldNote: Five years lets Olga **test before betting**, which fits her steady habit.
Her most personal change is **delaying children** until income is clearer.
She uses the **robot gap** for kitchen work as the household's main buffer.

steps.text: Cater weekend birthday dinners with Dario from next spring
Take a business and food-safety course by 2029
Delay starting a family until their income is clearer
Keep working and saving at Meridian until about 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives everyone a fair chance, so no excuses. Firms should start training now and governments should help pay for career changes. I'd be fairly upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be 37 when the thinking AI arrives. I could have a whole second career by then, or a business that's properly running. I'd probably still feel a bit sad about leaving insurance, because I've only just started getting good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the insurance certificate and try underwriting for a few years, use the AI tools more once they've proven themselves, and save. Around 2030 we'd decide about the catering business. And we'd probably start a family on the normal timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly okay. It feels like weather a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've only just started getting good. What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum's sticky notes have gone from five a file to one or two. I'm proud of that, small as it is. I'd hate to get good at insurance just as being good at insurance stops mattering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide for or against the catering business in 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Dario still loves cooking, and whether we've saved enough to survive a bad first year. If either answer's no, I'd look at something else hands-on, maybe dental nursing. I'd want two options, not one.

say: I'd say ten years gives everyone a **fair chance**, so no excuses.
Firms should **train now** and governments should help pay for **career changes**.
think: I'd be **37** with time for a second career or a running business.
I'd feel **sad** to leave insurance just as I'm getting good.
do: Pass the **insurance certificate** and try **underwriting** for a few years.
Use **AI tools** more once they've proven themselves.
Decide on the **catering business** with Dario around 2030.
feel: **Uneasy but mostly okay**, like weather a long way off.
S4.quote: I'd hate to get good at insurance just as being good at insurance stops mattering.
fieldNote: Ten years lets Olga **enjoy getting good** at insurance before leaving it.
She wants **two options**, catering or dental nursing, not a single bet.
Family plans stay on the **normal timeline**, unlike the five-year picture.

steps.text: Pass the insurance certificate and move into underwriting
Use Meridian's AI tools more once they've proven themselves
Wait until 2030 to decide on the catering business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of me alone, but because it would land on both of us at once, my job straight away and Dario's three years later. What would help is time, honestly: a rule that firms phase changes in over a couple of years, and an income for people while they switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about small businesses. The cafés and salons I insure run on thin margins, and if their insurance gets cheaper because of AI, that's good for them. I'd like someone to remember both sides of that.

headlineQuote: The cafés and salons I insure run on thin margins, and if their insurance gets cheaper because of AI, that's good for them.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old commercial policy clerk** handling small business renewals, still making slips.
She lives with Dario, a **chef** with unsteady shifts, and co-owns a **rented flat** with her sister.
Pragmatic and steady, she **learns from colleagues** first and avoids blaming anyone.
In the AGI pictures she plans a **catering business** with Dario, tested before any big bet.
Her mood runs from **uneasy** to **alarmed**, with hospitality worries present even if AI stalls.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would hit her job at once and Dario's three years later.
whatWouldHelp: A rule making firms **phase changes in** over a couple of years.
An **income** for people while they switch careers.
